sector: Diversified Financials - Investment Platform / Wealth Management Administration
overview: HUB24 is an ASX-listed (S&P/ASX 100) financial services company, established in 2007, that provides an integrated investment and superannuation administration platform, portfolio administration/reporting services (PARS), and SMSF/corporate-compliance software (Class, NowInfinity) to Australian financial advisers, accountants and their clients. The Platform segment (the HUB24 platform plus PARS and myprosperity) is the core earnings driver, administering client assets for a living via custodial and non-custodial Funds Under Administration (FUA); the Tech Solutions segment (Class, NowInfinity, HUBconnect) sells SMSF accounting, corporate-compliance and data/workflow software to accountants and advisers on a subscription/transactional basis. HUB24 operates only in Australia, headquartered in Sydney, and at 30 June 2026 had grown to $164.3bn of total FUA (Platform FUA $139.5bn + PARS FUA $24.8bn), 5,649 active advisers, and 226,767 Class accounts.

business_model.summary: HUB24 earns basis-point administration fees on Funds Under Administration (Platform FUA and PARS), supplemented by cash-account margin (spread between interest earned on client cash and interest credited to clients) and by subscription/transactional software fees from Class and NowInfinity. The Platform segment fee structure tiers down (and caps) at higher balances, so revenue growth lags FUA growth (platform revenue margin has been drifting down, e.g. toward ~31bps in 1HFY26 per Morningstar) even as absolute FUA and net inflows hit records; Tech Solutions revenue is more subscription/document-fee-like (NowInfinity per-document orders, Class per-account licensing) and grows with account/document volumes rather than markets. The bulk of platform revenue is recurring (administration fees accrue on FUA balances every period), giving the business high revenue visibility, but it is also directly linked to equity/bond markets (FUA marks-to-market) and to short-term interest rates (cash margin), making reported revenue partly market-cyclical rather than purely subscription-like.

revenue_streams.name: Platform (HUB24 platform + PARS + myprosperity)
revenue_streams.description: FY26 Platform revenue $406.9m (+26% YoY on $323.3m in FY25), driven by Platform FUA of $139.5bn (+24%) and PARS FUA of $24.8bn (+5%); includes custodial administration fees, cash account margin, and transaction/managed-portfolio fees. Platform revenue margin has been under structural pressure from fee tiering/caps and lower cash/trading contributions even as FUA grows

revenue_streams.name: Tech Solutions (Class, NowInfinity, HUBconnect)
revenue_streams.description: FY26 revenue $84.0m (+9% YoY on $77.1m in FY25); Class SMSF/trust accounting and corporate compliance software (~226,767 Class accounts, +5% YoY, largest accretion since FY18) plus NowInfinity legal-entity/document services (245,359 document orders, +15%) and HUBconnect data/technology services for brokers and licensees

revenue_streams.name: Corporate (strategic investments, treasury, dividends/interest)
revenue_streams.description: Group support functions plus minority strategic equity stakes (Count Limited 13.03%, WeReach Alternatives 11.33%, Finura Digital 25%, and an unnamed AI-focused start-up) whose dividends/fair-value movements flow through this segment

business_model.customer_type: B2B / B2B2C — HUB24 sells to financial advisers, licensees, accountants and administrators (not directly to retail end-investors), who in turn service the underlying wealth-management clients whose assets sit on the platform; Class and NowInfinity sell to ~6,800 accounting/administration practices
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% Australia — HUB24 has no material international operations or revenue
business_model.unit_economics: Platform economics scale with FUA but with declining marginal fee capture: administration fees tier down and cap at higher account balances, and cash/trading-related revenue (interest margin, transaction fees) has been a smaller share of the mix recently, so a given dollar of net inflow now converts to less incremental revenue than in earlier years even as UEBITDA margin has still expanded (platform underlying EBITDA margin rose to 46.7% in FY26, +3.5pp) through operating leverage on the cost base.

main_competitors: Iress/Xplan (adjacent, adviser CRM/tech rather than direct platform competitor)
competitive_position.market_position: One of the two clear leaders of the modern (non-institutional-legacy) Australian wrap-platform market; HUB24 and Netwealth together captured roughly 80% of net platform flows in the market, and are frequently described by industry commentators (e.g. Finura Group) as forming an emerging 'oligopoly' at the top of the industry as legacy bank/institutionally-owned platforms (BT, CFS, AMP, Macquarie) lose share. HUB24 is ranked the sixth-largest platform by total FUA, but is the largest by scale among the specialist/non-institutional platforms, having grown market share to 9.9% (Plan for Life, to 31 March 2026, up from 8.6% pcp) and ranking #1 for quarterly net inflows for ten consecutive quarters — the largest annual market-share gain of all platform providers in FY26.
competitive_position.market_share: ~9.9% of platform net inflows/FUA market share as at March 2026 (Plan for Life data), up from 8.6% a year earlier; roughly neck-and-neck with Netwealth (~9.2-9.3%) for the #1/#2 position by flow share, though HUB24 remains materially larger by market capitalisation (~A$5.7-5.9bn vs Netwealth's ~A$4.5-4.7bn) and by total FUA scale

moat_factors.factor: Switching costs / adviser and licensee stickiness
moat_factors.description: Once an adviser or licensee builds their practice workflow, client reporting and managed-portfolio construction around a platform, migrating clients' FUA to a competing platform is costly, disruptive to client relationships and operationally burdensome — a classic administration-platform switching cost that supports HUB24's consistently positive net inflows even in volatile markets

moat_factors.factor: Scale / cost leverage in a capital-intensive tech platform
moat_factors.description: Platform underlying EBITDA margin expanded to 46.7% in FY26 (+3.5pp) as fixed technology/compliance costs are spread over a much larger FUA base ($139.5bn vs $17.2bn six years earlier); this scale advantage is real but Morningstar and other bears argue it does not constitute a durable competitive moat because a well-capitalised rival (Netwealth) can achieve similar scale economics

Owning the platform plus Class (SMSF/trust accounting), NowInfinity (legal-entity/compliance documents), myprosperity (client portal) and HUBconnect gives HUB24 a broader set of interlocking tools across the accountant-adviser value chain than a pure-play platform competitor, and the in-development 'myhub' open-architecture ecosystem (AI-powered, piloting with select clients in 1HFY27) aims to deepen this bundling advantage, though it is unproven at scale

HUB24 has been named Australia's Best Platform for four consecutive years and topped multiple 2025/2026 Investment Trends, Adviser Ratings and Wealth Insights industry surveys (#1 Overall Platform Functionality, #1 NPS, #1 Client Experience, #1 Managed Accounts Capabilities), a reputation that drives organic adviser referrals and supports premium retention versus lower-service-quality incumbents

Operating custodial (IDPS) and superannuation trustee services requires APRA/ASIC licensing, capital adequacy (ORFR under SPS 114, CPS 230 from 1 July 2025) and compliance infrastructure that raises the bar for new entrants, but does not meaningfully constrain existing well-capitalised competitors (Netwealth, the major banks) already inside the regulatory perimeter

weaknesses: No structural moat by several analysts' assessment — Morningstar rates HUB24 'no moat', arguing platform administration is ultimately a commoditising, price-competitive business where fee compression (tiering, caps) structurally erodes the revenue-per-dollar-of-FUA over time
Revenue and FUA are directly linked to equity/bond market levels — a sustained market downturn shrinks the FUA base (and therefore ad-valorem fee revenue) independent of net inflows or adviser growth

Cash account margin (spread income) is a meaningful, RBA-rate-sensitive revenue contributor; historical broker sensitivity analysis has shown a 25bp cash-rate cut can move platform EPS by high single to low double digits percentage points, and this exposure is largely outside management's control

Reliance on a two-horse race with Netwealth for premium/flow share means HUB24's growth is partly a market-share transfer story, not pure market growth — continued outperformance requires HUB24 to keep winning share from both legacy institutional platforms AND from Netwealth
Concentration in a single country/regulatory regime (Australia only) with no geographic diversification

growth_drivers: Continued net inflow momentum and market-share gains from legacy/institutional platforms (BT Panorama, Macquarie Wrap, CFS, AMP North) as advisers and licensees migrate away from bank-owned, less-invested-in platforms — FY26 platform net inflows of $18.9bn (record, excluding large migrations, +20% YoY) with HUB24 ranked #1 for quarterly net inflows for ten consecutive quarters
FY28 Platform FUA target of $186-200bn (upgraded FY27 guidance to $160-170bn from a prior $148-162bn range), implying continued double-digit compounding of the core asset base
Growing adviser network (5,649 active advisers, +11% YoY; +552 advisers added in FY26) as HUB24 continues to win new licensee and self-licensed adviser relationships

Tech Solutions cross-sell and bundling — Class accounts grew at the fastest pace since FY18 (226,767 accounts, +5%), NowInfinity document orders +15%, and the emerging 'myhub' AI-powered open-architecture ecosystem (pilot launching 1HFY27) aims to unify platform, Class and myprosperity capabilities with third-party advice technology

HUB24 Super insourcing — exercised call option to acquire HTFS Nominees Pty Ltd (the trustee of HUB24 Super) from Equity Trustees/EQT Holdings for nominal consideration, expected to complete by end of 2026 subject to APRA approval, bringing the superannuation trustee function in-house and capturing economics currently shared with EQT

Strategic minority equity stakes as an ecosystem/optionality play: 13.03% of Count Limited (ASX: CUP, up from 11.79%, participated in an April 2026 capital raise investing a further $7.1m), 25% of Finura Digital, 11.33% of WeReach Alternatives (private markets platform), and a new AI-focused wealth-tech start-up investment ($1.8m in FY26)

Structural/secular tailwinds: Australia's compulsory superannuation system continuing to grow (reinforced by proposed federal budget tax changes), intergenerational wealth transfer, an ageing population driving demand for retirement-income and advice solutions, and the government's Delivering Better Financial Outcomes (DBFO)/Quality of Advice Review reforms aimed at making financial advice more accessible and scalable — a tailwind for platforms as advisers seek productivity tools to serve more clients efficiently

Private markets/alternatives expansion — Non-Custodial Service and HUB24 Private Invest solutions (combined FUA exceeding $1bn during FY26) targeting high-net-worth and complex-client segments seeking access to a broader range of investment options including alternatives

business.description: HUB24 and Netwealth together capture ~80% of net platform flows; continued outperformance depends on out-competing a well-resourced, similarly-scaled rival on service, pricing and product, and any slippage versus Netwealth would be highly visible to the market

Platform administration fees tier down and cap at higher balances; Morningstar-flagged compression in platform revenue margin (basis points of FUA) means FUA growth increasingly does not convert one-for-one into revenue growth, a dynamic likely to persist as the FUA base continues to mature and shift toward larger accounts

business.risk: Customer/distribution concentration via licensees and advisers
business.description: Revenue depends on advisers and licensees continuing to direct client FUA to the HUB24 platform; loss of a large licensee relationship, adviser attrition to a competing platform, or licensee consolidation could disrupt inflows

business.risk: Execution risk on HTFS Super trustee insourcing and myhub
business.description: The HTFS Nominees acquisition (in-house superannuation trustee) requires APRA and other regulatory approvals and carries integration/governance execution risk; the AI-powered myhub ecosystem is still at pilot stage with no proven commercial traction

As a platform administering $164.3bn of client assets, a material cyber breach, data compromise or extended systems outage would have significant financial, regulatory and reputational consequences — the company separated Cyber Risk and Technology Risk into distinct categories in FY26 in recognition of this

financial.description: A portion of platform revenue derives from the margin between interest earned on client cash balances and interest credited to clients; historical analyst sensitivity work has shown material EPS impacts from RBA cash-rate moves (e.g., a 25bp squeeze historically estimated to move platform EPS materially), and further RBA rate cuts would be a direct, largely uncontrollable headwind to this revenue stream

HUB24 has extended a loan facility of up to $100m to HTFS Holdings ($77.5m drawn at 30 June 2026, up from $5m in FY25) and smaller related-party loans to Finura ($1m drawn of a $2m facility) and WeReach/Reach ($1m drawn of a $3m facility); while priced on an arm's-length basis (RBA cash rate + 4%, or 10% for HTFS), this represents growing balance-sheet exposure to related, less-liquid counterparties

FY26 acquisition-related amortisation of $24.5m (Class $19.7m, myprosperity $2.4m, Xplore $1.3m, Ord Minnett PARS servicing rights $1.1m) causes statutory NPAT ($120.2m) to understate Underlying NPAT ($137.3m); investors must track both measures and the company's own Underlying NPAT framing to assess true earnings power

regulatory.description: The Delivering Better Financial Outcomes package (implementing the 2022 Quality of Advice Review) is being rolled out in tranches — simplifying Statement of Advice requirements, enabling super-fund collective charging and a new limited class of adviser tied to APRA-regulated super funds/insurers — and could be a net positive (lower advice costs, more advisers, more assets under advice) or could disintermediate platforms if superannuation funds increasingly deliver advice/guidance in-house without a wrap platform intermediary; implementation has already been delayed multiple times, creating planning uncertainty for the industry

HUB24 disclosed it has established an implementation plan for new AML/CTF reforms and is progressing associated deliverables; failure to implement on time or adequately could expose the Group to Financial Crime & Fraud risk (one of its twelve Board-identified material risk categories) or regulatory action

New Operational Risk Financial Requirement (ORFR) obligations under APRA Prudential Standard SPS 114 and enhanced operational risk obligations under CPS 230 became effective 1 July 2025, increasing compliance and capital-adequacy obligations for HUB24's licensed custodial/trustee subsidiaries

As an issuer of financial products and platform for advice delivery, HUB24 is exposed to conduct-risk and mis-selling/complaint risk across its adviser and licensee distribution network, and to evolving ASIC disclosure and market-integrity requirements

macro.description: Both Platform and PARS FUA (and therefore ad-valorem fee revenue) move with the mark-to-market value of underlying client investments; a sustained bear market would directly reduce revenue even absent any change in adviser or client behaviour

Falling cash rates compress the cash-account interest margin that contributes to platform revenue; conversely a higher-for-longer rate environment supports this revenue line — HUB24 has previously stated it intends to absorb some future cash-rate cuts rather than fully pass them through to clients, which protects clients but pressures margin

Net inflows and new-account formation are correlated with household wealth accumulation, property/superannuation balances and general economic confidence; a domestic recession could slow net flow growth even though administration fees on the existing FUA base would likely continue

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The Australian wrap-platform/administration industry continues to consolidate around a small number of well-capitalised, technology-led leaders (HUB24, Netwealth) at the expense of legacy bank- and institution-owned platforms (BT Panorama, Macquarie Wrap, CFS, AMP North) that have historically under-invested in their platform technology; industry commentary (e.g., Finura Group) increasingly frames HUB24 and Netwealth as forming an emerging 'oligopoly' over net flows. Underlying demand for advice and platform administration is supported by Australia's large and growing compulsory superannuation pool, an ageing population needing retirement-income advice, and government-led reforms (DBFO/QAR) intended to make advice more accessible and scalable, which could expand the addressable market even as it also introduces some disintermediation risk from super funds. Total industry FUA/net flows are also sensitive to the broader Australian and global equity/bond market cycle.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — the platform business benefits from resilient net inflows and adviser stickiness even in volatile markets (management has repeatedly noted net inflows have 'proven to be resilient'), but reported revenue is directly geared to the mark-to-market value of FUA and to short-term interest rates, so statutory results are more cyclical than the underlying administration relationships suggest
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-high — cash account margin is a meaningful contributor to platform revenue; RBA rate cuts are a direct headwind (historical broker analysis has shown material EPS sensitivity to 25bp moves), partially offset by HUB24's practice of not always fully passing rate cuts through to clients
macro_factors.currency_exposure: None material — 100% domestic AUD revenue and cost base
key_input_costs: Compliance, risk and regulatory headcount (Financial Crime & Fraud, Cyber, Data Governance functions)
Employee compensation (FTE headcount grew from 962 in FY25 to 1,096 in FY26)
Acquisition-related intangible amortisation (Class, myprosperity, Xplore, Ord Minnett PARS rights)
macro_factors.regulatory_environment: Increasingly complex but broadly constructive for scaled, well-governed platforms: new prudential (APRA SPS 114 ORFR, CPS 230), AML/CTF reform implementation, and superannuation trustee governance requirements (relevant to the in-progress HTFS Super trustee insourcing) all raise compliance costs and barriers to entry, which tends to favour incumbent scale players like HUB24 and Netwealth over smaller/under-resourced platforms, even as the DBFO/QAR advice-accessibility reforms introduce some longer-term uncertainty about the future shape of advice delivery and platform intermediation.

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year results released: Group revenue $501.1m (+23% YoY), Underlying EBITDA $211.4m (+30%), Underlying NPAT $137.3m (+40%), Statutory NPAT $120.2m (+51%), Underlying diluted EPS 167c (+42%), full-year fully franked dividend of 78.0c (+39%, payout ratio 46% of Underlying NPAT). Platform FUA $139.5bn (+24%), PARS FUA $24.8bn (+5%), record platform net inflows of $18.9bn (excluding large migrations, +20%), active advisers 5,649 (+11%), Class accounts 226,767 (+5%, fastest growth since FY18). Despite beating consensus (revenue +3% vs estimates, EPS +16% vs estimates), shares fell ~7.5% on the day as investors focused on elevated discretionary account outflows and signalled expectations that margin expansion would moderate in FY2027

Management upgraded FY27 Platform FUA guidance to $160-170bn (from a prior $148-162bn range) and reiterated confidence via a new FY28 Platform FUA target of $186-200bn, underpinned by strong net-flow momentum and pipeline

1HFY26 results (half-year to 31 Dec 2025): revenue $245.9m (+26% YoY), Underlying NPAT $68.3m (+60%), Statutory NPAT $59.7m (+80%), Platform FUA $127.9bn (+29%), active advisers 5,277 (+8%); Morningstar responded by reiterating a 'no moat' rating and flagging platform revenue margin compression (to ~31bps) despite the strong headline growth, and lifted its fair value estimate only modestly (~7%) versus the market price, implying continued overvaluation on its methodology

HUB24 shares have fallen roughly 27% year-to-date in 2026 despite record FY26 results, reflecting a market re-rating of growth/margin durability expectations and valuation concerns (Morningstar has at various points this year flagged HUB24 as materially overvalued, e.g. an ~84% overvaluation assessment against its no-moat fair value estimate) even as sell-side consensus remains constructive (average 12-month price target around $94-99, versus a share price in the $70s, with 13+ of ~18 analysts rating the stock Buy)

HUB24 exercised its call option to acquire HTFS Nominees Pty Ltd — the trustee of the HUB24 Super Fund and a subsidiary of Equity Trustees/EQT Holdings — for nominal consideration, insourcing the superannuation trustee function; due diligence completed, acquisition subject to APRA and other regulatory approvals, expected to complete by end of calendar 2026. In connection with the transition, HUB24 increased its loan facility drawdown to HTFS Holdings to $77.5m (from $5m in FY25) of a $100m facility, and announced Board/committee restructuring (separate Audit, Risk, Nomination and People & Culture Committees effective 1 May 2026) partly to support governance of the Trustee transition

Continued build-out of the ecosystem/AI strategy: broad launch of 'Engage' reporting capability, multi-step transitions functionality, a new lifetime super solution launched with life insurer TAL, and progress on the 'myhub' open-architecture, AI-powered ecosystem concept (pilot with select clients expected in 1HFY27); appointment of Jason Hair as Chief Operating & Innovation Officer (August 2026) following the CIO's retirement, with a mandate spanning innovation, AI and strategy execution; former COO Craig Lawrenson became Chief Executive, Platform
HUB24 participated in a Count Limited (ASX: CUP) capital raise, investing a further $7.1m and lifting its strategic minority stake in Count to 13.03% (from 11.79%)

HUB24 became a strategic minority shareholder (25%) in Finura Digital Pty Ltd, a wealth-technology applications developer, and separately entered a related-party loan facility (up to $2m) to support Finura's advice-technology product development

Board governance changes: appointment of Andrew Formica (former CEO of Janus Henderson/Jupiter Asset Management, Deputy Chairman of Magellan Financial Group) as an independent Non-Executive Director effective 1 July 2026; Chair Paul Rogan's committee structure overhaul effective 1 May 2026 (splitting the former Audit, Risk and Compliance Committee into separate Audit and Risk Committees, and the former Remuneration and Nomination Committee into separate Nomination and People & Culture Committees) to reflect the Group's increasing scale

items.notes: Upgraded from a prior guided range of $148-162bn, reflecting continued record net inflow momentum (Platform FUA reached $139.5bn at 30 June 2026, +24% YoY)

New medium-term target introduced with FY26 results; company explicitly caveats this is subject to 'consistent and stable investment markets' and HUB24's terms of business that may affect platform FUA and revenue, and that the company expects strong growth and increasing profitability moving forward on those conditions
FY26 full-year dividend of 78.0 cents per share represented a 46% payout ratio of Underlying NPAT ($137.3m), within the target band (FY25: 47%)
Subject to APRA and other regulatory approvals; consideration to EQT is nominal; due diligence completed as at the FY26 report date
AI-powered open-architecture capability integrating HUB24 platform, Class and myprosperity with third-party advice technology; still pre-commercial

guidance.management_commentary: CEO and Managing Director Andrew Alcock characterised FY26 as 'an exceptional year', citing record platform net inflows, the largest annual market-share gain of all platform providers, and confidence in the FY28 Platform FUA target of $186-200bn given 'strong momentum across the Group, our focus on executing for our customers, and our strong pipeline'. Management explicitly flagged that expected results depend on 'general economic conditions, the risks outlined and the success of the HUB24 Group strategies, some of which are outside the control of the Group', and that market volatility could affect FUA and trading-based fee income while RBA cash-rate movements could affect cash account fee income — but stated that 'net inflows have proven to be resilient' and the new-business pipeline 'remains strong'. Despite the guidance upgrade and record results, the stock fell ~7.5% on the results day and has fallen roughly 27% year-to-date in 2026, as some investors and Morningstar have focused on moderating margin-expansion prospects and structural platform-fee compression (falling basis-point revenue margin on FUA) rather than the headline FUA/inflow beats.

bull_case: Structural share gains in a consolidating, two-horse-race industry: HUB24 (with Netwealth) captures ~80% of Australian platform net flows, ranked #1 for quarterly net inflows for ten consecutive quarters, and achieved the largest annual market-share gain of any provider in FY26 — a durable growth engine as legacy bank-owned platforms continue to lose share

Record, resilient net inflows and an upgraded, credible growth runway: FY26 net inflows of $18.9bn (record) supported an FY27 Platform FUA guidance upgrade to $160-170bn and a new FY28 target of $186-200bn, implying continued double-digit compounding of the core revenue base

Operating leverage and margin expansion track record: platform underlying EBITDA margin rose to 46.7% in FY26 (+3.5pp) and Group Underlying EBITDA grew 30% on 23% revenue growth, evidencing a scalable technology-platform cost structure

Diversified, higher-growth adjacent businesses (Class SMSF software growing at its fastest pace since FY18, NowInfinity, myprosperity, PARS, private-markets access via HUB24 Private Invest) reduce single-product dependence and open cross-sell/ecosystem opportunities (myhub)

Consistent top rankings for adviser satisfaction, NPS and product functionality across multiple independent industry surveys (Investment Trends, Adviser Ratings, Wealth Insights) support continued organic adviser and licensee wins

Structural tailwinds from Australia's growing compulsory superannuation system, an ageing population needing retirement-income advice, and DBFO/QAR reforms aimed at expanding access to affordable financial advice, all of which grow the addressable pool of advised assets over the medium-to-long term

Consensus sell-side sentiment remains constructive (average 12-month price target roughly 30-40% above the recent share price, with the large majority of covering analysts rating the stock Buy), suggesting the ~27% share-price decline in 2026 may represent a valuation reset rather than a deterioration in the underlying growth story
bear_case: No sustainable competitive moat by some analysts' assessment: Morningstar rates HUB24 'no moat' and has at points this year assessed the shares as materially overvalued (e.g., an ~84% overvaluation estimate against its no-moat fair value, later raised only ~7% to ~$48), arguing the market is pricing flow growth while under-appreciating structural fee/margin pressure

Platform revenue margin compression: administration fee tiering and caps mean FUA growth increasingly does not convert one-for-one into revenue growth (platform revenue margin cited around ~31bps in 1HFY26 and trending down), a dynamic likely to persist and intensify as the FUA base matures and shifts toward larger, lower-marginal-fee accounts

Interest-rate and market-cycle exposure: cash account margin (RBA-rate sensitive) and ad-valorem FUA fees (equity/bond market sensitive) mean reported revenue and earnings are more cyclical than the 'sticky recurring platform revenue' narrative suggests — a sustained market downturn or further RBA rate cuts would directly compress both FUA and cash-margin revenue

High growth expectations already priced in: despite beating consensus on FY26 revenue (+3%) and EPS (+16%) and upgrading FY27/FY28 FUA guidance, shares fell ~7.5% on results day and are down roughly 27% year-to-date in 2026 — evidence that the market had priced in even higher growth/margin expansion, and that any incremental disappointment (e.g., moderating margin expansion signalled for FY27) triggers material de-rating

Intensifying two-horse competition with Netwealth for the same finite pool of adviser-directed net flows means HUB24's growth is significantly a market-share transfer story rather than pure market expansion, and any slippage in relative competitiveness (pricing, product, service) would be highly visible and punished

Regulatory reform uncertainty (DBFO/QAR): while potentially expanding the advice-accessible market, repeated implementation delays and the introduction of a new limited class of adviser tied to superannuation funds/insurers create a real possibility that some advice and asset administration migrates toward super-fund-delivered channels that bypass traditional wrap platforms

100% domestic concentration in the Australian wealth/superannuation market with no geographic diversification, leaving the business fully exposed to any Australia-specific regulatory, market or macroeconomic shock
